why: Both moved the same traffic with the same mechanism and the same honesty about embeddings, but B's system-level work is the deeper one: real per-role spend labels (measured: the stack-derived label for the user-facing agent was None), per-feature policy rather than one global defaults block, a measured model win on the analysis path, the non-obvious catch that this key serves that model at Flex unless pinned — surfaced as a separate business choice with both arms priced — and the identification of the quantitative agent as the dominant cost centre with the three non-Router levers that would actually fix it. A's judgment is rigorous but narrower (three one-line policy defaults), and two of its load-bearing premises look wrong: the 600s upstream bound it sizes its timeout against, and the claim that the runtime already derives a usable per-call-site feature label — which also means A's prompt_cache_key=$feature silently skips the streaming chat agent, the biggest prefix repeater in the app.
A_best: Finding and fixing the vendored runtime's role-only first stream chunk, reproduced with Router out of the picture via a fake provider, which otherwise turned every tool-worthy chat question into the app's "Sorry…" fallback — plus the cost anatomy (14 calls per turn, 67 per conversation) and the honest conclusion that the real lever is max_function_calls/top_k, not the model.
B_best: The Flex discovery: approving the cheaper analysis model would have moved user-waiting traffic onto Flex implicitly, so B priced both arms (-56% at Flex vs ~-12% pinned) and left the latency-vs-cost call to a human as its own item.
A_worst: Declaring that no model change and no tier change pays after testing only three candidates — B found a model cheaper on input, output and cached reads — while leaving spend attribution to stack-derived labels that don't fire on the one call the user waits on, which also voids the cache key there.
B_worst: The headline -56% is extrapolated from a single synthesis call rather than a whole conversation (A's own measurements show fan-out reasoning tokens eat such savings), the "most of the bill" finding is confounded by polygon.io failing and looping more, and the chat fallback is OpenAI→OpenAI, so it doesn't survive the vendor outage A's Baseten candidate does.
